content.comment_body: What is the highest version of [product_name] that allows program download from a [product_name] controller ([article_no])? Should I use [product_name] version 6 or version 8.3?
Any [product_name] version equal to or greater than version 6 is compatible with [product_name] [article_no].

Ideally, you should have an offline backup of your program as a base. Uploading directly from the [product_name] controller often results in a cluttered wiring view. Having the specific programming cable (serial or USB) is also necessary.

Working from an offline program is preferable to reading directly from the [product_name] controller. In [product_name] version 6, only the binary program is saved—no structure, symbols, or comments. Since Windows 11 hasn't been fully tested or released for [product_name] use, I recommend running Windows 7, 8, or 10 alongside [product_name] version 8.3. The manufacturer no longer sells the programming cable, but perhaps someone still has access to one.

These recommendations aren't ideal for customers, especially since Windows 10 will reach end-of-life in 2025. Requiring a CD or DVD drive to install newly purchased software is even more inconvenient. Most [product_name] users are outside the traditional industrial automation sector, so these requirements seem outdated.

The problems with Windows 11 can't be blamed solely on [company_name]. Many niche software providers are facing similar issues. Microsoft keeps updating the OS frequently, making it hard for software vendors to catch up. Windows 11, which essentially builds on Windows 10, has many bugs and its updates have been continuous. Microsoft is likely to release Windows 12 as Windows 10 reaches the end-of-life in 2025—expected sometime in 2024. We'll have to wait and see.

[Opinion] Your view is valid—Windows 11 remains problematic. That's likely why [product_name] was initially developed using Java; the Java virtual machine was supposed to function as a bridge between Windows and the application. However, Oracle's move to monetize Java use for companies complicates matters. Most new PCs today are shipped with Windows 11 Home Edition. Many non-industrial users will have this OS on their computers, though only a handful use Apple devices. The lack of official certification for [product_name] on specific Windows 11 builds seems like a business oversight.

Completely agree. The bigger issue may be between Oracle and Microsoft. For years, buying a new computer typically means getting Windows by default, with Microsoft controlling both hardware requirements and user data access. Reading the terms and conditions reveals just how many rights are handed over to Microsoft. There’s also a significant security gap overlooked by many protection programs. Those prioritizing privacy and data security should consider alternatives, as learning a new OS can be as easy as adapting to a new Windows release.
